### Cloning and general methods

Plasmids were constructed by using Q5 DNA Polymerase (NEB) to amplify fragments that were then ligated via Gibson Assembly. Primers were obtained from IDT, and all plasmids were sequenced at the University of Chicago Comprehensive Cancer Center DNA Sequencing and Genotyping Facility. Vectors and gene sequences used in this study are listed in Supplementary file 5, with links to fully annotated vector maps on Benchling. Key vectors are deposited at Addgene, and all vectors are available upon request. The following working concentrations of antibiotics were used: 50 µg/mL carbenicillin, 50 µg/mL spectinomycin, 40 µg/mL kanamycin, and 33 µg/mL chloramphenicol. Protein structures and alignments were generated using the program PyMOL (Schrödinger, 2018).

### Luciferase assay

Cloned expression vectors contained the following: (1) a previously evolved, isopropyl β-D-1-thiogalactopyranoside (IPTG)-inducible N-terminal half of T7 RNAP (Zinkus-Boltz et al., 2019) fused to a BCL-2 family protein; (2) the C-terminal half of T7 RNAP fused to a peptide from a BH3-only protein; and (3) T7 promoter-driven luciferase reporter. Chemically competent S1030 E. coli cells (Carlson et al., 2014) were prepared by culturing to an OD600 of 0.3, washing twice with a calcium chloride/HEPES solution (60 mM CaCl2, 10 mM HEPES pH 7.0, 15% glycerol), and then resuspending in the same solution. Vectors were transformed into chemically competent S1030 cells via heat shock at 42°C for 45 s, followed by 1 hr recovery in 3× volume of 2xYT media, and then plated on agar with the appropriate antibiotics (carbenicillin, spectinomycin, and chloramphenicol) to incubate overnight at 37°C. Individual colonies (three to four biological replicates per condition) were picked and cultured in 1 mL of LB media containing the appropriate antibiotics overnight at 37°C in a shaker. The next morning, 50 µL of each culture was diluted into 450 µL of fresh LB media containing the appropriate antibiotics, as well as 1 µM of IPTG. The cells were incubated in a shaker at 37°C, and OD600 and luminescence measurements were recorded between 2.5 and 4.5 hr after the start of the incubation. Measurements were taken on a Synergy Neo2 Microplate Reader (BioTek) by transferring 150 µL of the daytime cultures into Corning black, clear-bottom 96-well plates. Data were analyzed in Microsoft Excel and plotted in GraphPad Prism, as previously reported (Pu et al., 2017a).

Protein expression hsBCL-2, hsMCL-1, and evolved variants were constructed as N-terminal 6xHis-GST tagged proteins. The recombinant proteins were expressed in BL21 E. coli (NEB) and purified following standard Ni-NTA resin purification protocols (ThermoFisher Scientific) (Zhou et al., 2019). Briefly, BL21 E. coli containing an N-terminal 6xHis-GST tagged BCL-2 family protein were cultured in 5 mL LB with carbenicillin overnight. The following day, the culture was added to 0.5 L of LB with carbenicillin, incubated at 37°C until it reached an OD600 of 0.6, induced with IPTG (final concentration: 200 µM), and cultured overnight at 16°C. The cell pellet was harvested by centrifugation followed by resuspension in 30 mL of lysis buffer (50 mM Tris 1 M NaCl, 20% glycerol, 10 mM TCEP, pH 7.5) supplemented by protease inhibitors (200 nM Aprotinin, 10 µM Bestatin, 20 µM E-64, 100 µM Leupeptin, 1 mM AEBSF, 20 µM Pepstatin A). Cells were lysed via sonication and were then centrifuged at 12,000 g for 40 min at 4°C. Solubilized proteins, located in the supernatant, were incubated with His60 Ni Superflow Resin (Takara) for 1 hr at 4°C, and the protein was eluted using a gradient of imidazole in lysis buffer (50–250 mM). Fractions with the protein, as determined by SDS-PAGE, were concentrated in Ulta-50 Centrifugal Filter Units (Amicon, EMD Millipore). Proteins were purified via a desalting column with storage buffer (50 mM Tris–HCl [pH 7.5], 300 mM NaCl, 10% glycerol, 1 mM DTT) and further concentrated. The concentration of the purified BCL-2 family proteins was determined by BCA assay (ThermoFisher Scientific), and they were flash-frozen in liquid nitrogen and stored at −80°C.

### Fluorescent polarization binding assays

Fluorescent polarization (FP) was used to measure the affinity of BCL-2 family proteins with peptide fragments of the BH3-only proteins in accordance with previously described methods (Zhang et al., 2002). hsBCL-2, hsMCL-1, and evolved variants were purified as described above. The fluorescent NOXA and BID peptides (95+% purity) were synthesized by GenScript and were N-terminally labeled with 5-FAM-Ahx and C-terminally modified by amidation. These peptides were dissolved and stored in DMSO. Corning black, clear-bottom 384-well plates were used to measure FP, and three replicates were prepared for each data point. Each well contained the following 100 µL reaction: 20 nM BH3-only protein, 0.05 nM to 3 µM of BCL-2 family protein (1/3 serial dilutions), 20 mM Tris (pH 7.5), 100 mM NaCl, 1 mM EDTA, and 0.05% pluronic F-68. FP values (in milli-polarization units; mFP) of each sample were read by a Synergy Neo2 Microplate Reader (BioTek) with the FP 108 filter (485/530) at room temperature 5–15 min after mixing all the components. Data were analyzed in GraphPad Prism 8, using the following customized fitting equation, to calculate Kd (Zhou et al., 2019):

$$
y=B+C(D+K_{d}+x-\sqrt{D+K_{d}+x^{2}-4Dx})
$$

where y is normalized measured FP, x is the concentration of BCL-2 protein, D is the concentration of the BH3-only protein, B and C are parameters related to the FP value of free and bound BH3-only protein, and Kd is the dissociation constant.

### Phage-assisted continuous evolution

PACE was used to evolve hsBCL-2, hsMCL-1, and ancestral proteins in accord with previously reported technical methods (Carlson et al., 2014; Esvelt et al., 2011; Pu et al., 2019; Pu et al., 2017b) using a new vector system. Briefly, combinations of accessory plasmids and the MP6 mutagenesis plasmid (Badran and Liu, 2015) were transformed into S1030 E. coli., plated on agar containing the appropriate antibiotics (carbenicillin, kanamycin, and chloramphenicol) and 10 mM glucose, and incubated overnight at 37°C. Colonies were grown overnight in 5 mL of LB containing the appropriate antibiotics and 20 mM glucose. Davis Rich media was prepared in 5–10 L carboys and autoclaved, and the PACE flasks and corresponding pump tubing were autoclaved as well. The following day, PACE was set up in a 37°C environmental chamber (Forma 3960 environmental chamber, ThermoFisher Scientific). For each replicate, an overnight culture was added to ~150 mL of Davis Rich carboy media in chemostats and grown for 2–3 hr until reaching an OD600 of approximately 0.6. Lagoons containing 20 µL of phage from saturated phage stocks (108–109 phage) were then connected to the chemostat. Magnetic stir bars were used to agitate chemostats and lagoons. The chemostat cultures were flowed into the lagoons at a rate of approximately 20 mL/h. Waste output flow rates were adjusted to maintain a constant volume of 20 mL in the lagoons, 150 mL in the chemostat, and an OD600 close to 0.6 in the chemostat. A 10% w/v arabinose solution was pumped into the lagoons at a rate of 1 mL/h. If the experiment included a mixing step (two separate chemostats flowed together into one lagoon for a mixed selection pressure), a chemostat was prepared the next day (as described above) and connected to the lagoons. During this step, lagoon volumes were increased to 40 mL, and the arabinose inflow rate was increased to 2 mL/h. After disconnecting the first chemostat the next day, the lagoon volumes and arabinose inflow were both lowered to 20 mL and 1 mL/h, respectively. During the experiment, samples were collected from the lagoons every 24 hr and centrifuged at 13,000 rpm for 3 min to collect the phage-containing supernatant, as well as the cell pellet for DNA extraction. PACE experiments are listed in Supplementary file 3. A single replicate of AncB5 was removed because of contamination. No statistical method was used to determine the number of replicates as only four independent replicate experiments could be performed simultaneously.

During PACE, the media volume of each lagoon turned over once per hour for 4 days, or ~100 times. For a phage population to survive this amount of dilution, a similar number of generations must have occurred between the starting phage and the phage in the lagoon at the end of the experiment (Esvelt et al., 2011). This is expected to be a conservative estimate; as a more fit phage rises in frequency in the population, it will undergo a greater number of generations than less-fit phage in the population. The mutagenesis plasmid MP6 induces a mutation rate of approximately 6 × 10−6 per bp per generation. The BCL2 family proteins used in the PACE experiments were ~230 amino acids long, indicating that a mutation occurred on average every ~250 phage replications. Phage population sizes ranged from 105 per mL to 1010 per mL over the course of a PACE experiment, indicating a rate of 400–40,000,000 new mutations every generation. Conservative estimates thus suggest that a during each individual replicate, phage populations sampled at least 40,000 mutations, and upwards of 4 × 109 mutations. While not all mutations were equally likely each generation because MP6 enriches for transitions (i.e. G→A, A→G, C→T, and T→C), the high number of mutations sampled suggests that the vast majority of possible single point mutations (approximately 230*3*4 = 2760 potential mutations) were sampled over the course of each experiment, with higher population sizes generating all potential single point mutations each generation.

### Plaque assays

Plaque assays were performed on 1059 E. coli cells (Carlson et al., 2014; Hubbard et al., 2015), which supply gene III (gIII) to phage in an activity-independent manner, to measure phage titers. Additionally, activity-dependent plaque assays were done on S1030 E. coli containing the desired accessory plasmids to determine the number of phage encoding a BCL-2 family protein with a given peptide-binding profile. All cells were grown to an OD600 of approximately 0.6 during the day. Four serial dilutions were done in Eppendorf tubes by serially pipetting 1 μL of phage into 50 µL of cells to yield the following dilutions: 1/50, 1/2500, 1/125,000, and 1/6,250,000. 650 µL of top agar (0.7% agar with LB media) was added to each tube, which was then immediately spread onto a quad plate containing bottom agar (1.5% agar with LB media). Plates were incubated overnight at 37°C. Plaques were counted the following day, and plaque forming units (PFU) per mL was calculated using the following equation:

$$
PFU=1000*A*50^{4-B}
$$

Where A is the number of plaques in a given quadrant, and B is the quadrant number where the phage were counted, in which one is the least dilute quadrant and four is the most dilute quadrant.

### Phage growth assays

Phage growth assays were performed by adding the following to a culture tube and shaking at 37°C for 6 hr: 1 mL of LB with the appropriate antibiotics (carbenicillin and kanamycin), 10 µL of saturated S1030 E. coli containing the accessory plasmids of interest, and ~1000 phage. Phage were then isolated by centrifugation at 13,000 rpm for 3 min, and PFU was determined by plaque assays using 1059 E. coli and the plaque assay protocol described above.

### High-throughput sequencing library construction

PACE samples were collected from each lagoon every 24 hr. The lagoon samples were centrifuged at 13,000 rpm for 3 min on a bench top centrifuge to separate supernatant and cell pellet. The phage-containing supernatants were stored at 4°C prior to the creation of sequencing libraries. To prepare Illumina sequencing libraries, each phage sample was cultured overnight with 1059 E. coli cells, followed by phage DNA purification (Qiagen plasmid purification reagent buffer), P1 (catalog number 19051), P2 (catalog number 19052), N3 (catalog number 19064), PE (catalog number 19065), and spin column for DNA (EconoSpin, catalog number 1920–250). The resulting DNA concentration was ~50 ng/µL. Freshly generated DNA samples were then used as template for PCR amplification. For each library sample, we amplified three overlapping fragments of the BCL-2 family protein, which are 218–241 bp in length (Figure 4—figure supplement 1). Each primer also included 6–9 ‘N’s to introduce length variation (Supplementary file 4). In total, 12 PCRs were used for each library. Phusion DNA polymerases and buffers (ThermoFisher Scientific, catalog number F518L) were used in the first PCR round to amplify all three fragments for all library sequencing. The 25 µL reaction contained: 0.5 µL of 50 mM MgCl2, 0.75 µL of 10 mM dNTP, 0.75 µL Phusion DNA polymerase, 20 ng library DNA, and 0.5 µL of 10 µM primer (each). The PCR were run on a C1000 Touch Thermal Cycler (Bio-Rad), with the following parameters: 98°C for 1 min, followed by 16 cycles of 98°C for 12 s, 58°C for 15 s and 72°C for 45 s, and finally 72°C for 5 min. PCR were purified using the ZYMO DNA clean and concentrator kit (catalog number D4013) and 96 well filter plate (EconoSpin, catalog number 2020–001). The DNA products were dissolved in 30 µL ddH2O. All 12 reactions for each library were combined, and 1 µL was used as the template for a second PCR round. PCR components and thermocycler parameters were the same as above, except that the annealing temperature was 56°C, and only 15 rounds of amplification were conducted. The primer and sample combinations are listed in Supplementary file 4. PCRs were then purified following the same procedure as previous step. Equal volumes of all 72 library samples were combined and concentration was measured using a Qubit 4 Fluorometer. The total DNA sample was 2.68 ng/µL (equivalent to 10 nM, according to the average length of PCR fragments). DNA samples were diluted to 4 nM from step 4 following the Illumina MiSeq System Denature and Dilute Libraries Guide and then diluted to 12 pM for high-throughput sequencing. The final sample contained 100 µL of 20 pM PhiX spike-in plus 500 µL of the 12 pM library sample. Sequencing was performed on the Illumina MiSeq System using MiSeq Reagent Kit v3 (600-cycle) with paired-end reads according to the manufacturer’s instructions.

### Processing of Illumina data

Illumina sequencing yielded 22 million reads, 13 million of which could be matched to a specific sample (Supplementary file 4). One replicate for AncB5 was found to be contaminated and removed from further analysis. To process the remaining data, we first used Trim Galore with default settings to trim reads based on quality (https://www.bioinformatics.babraham.ac.uk/projects/trim_galore/). Then, we used BBMerge, a script in BBTools (https://jgi.doe.gov/data-and-tools/bbtools/), to merge paired-end reads. Next, we used Clumpify to remove repeated barcode sequences. We then used Seal to identify and bin reads by sample and fragment. Finally, we used BBDuk to remove any primer or adapter sequence present. Scripts and reference sequences are available on Github (Thornton, 2021).

### Illumina sequencing analysis

Reads were binned by experiment and then aligned to the appropriate WT sequence using Geneious (low sensitivity, five iterations, gaps allowed). Sequences were then processed in R to remove sequences containing ‘N’s or that were not full length. Insertions found in less than 1% of the population and sites that extended outside of the coding region were removed from all sequences. Remaining gaps were standardized among replicates and within an experiment. Finally, allele frequencies were calculated for each site and amino acid, as well as remaining insertions and deletions.

### Quantifying the effects of chance and contingency on the outcomes of evolution

#### Estimating the effects of chance

Allele frequency differences among replicates started from the same genotype can only be caused by chance events. Thus, to determine the effects of chance ($C_{1}$) on the outcomes of evolution, we compared allele frequencies from replicate PACE experiments started from the same genotype. We compared allele frequencies of individual replicates to the average allele frequencies among replicates started from the same genotype by estimating the probability that two randomly chosen alleles would be different, i.e. the genetic variance, for each replicate individually ($V_{r}$) and the pooled sample of all replicates from a given starting genotype ($V_{g})$:

$$
C_{1}≡\frac{V_{g}}{V_{r}}=\frac{1-Q_{g}}{1-Q_{r}}
$$

where $Q_{r}$ is the probability that two randomly chosen alleles in the same replicate are identical in state and $Q_{g}$ is the probability that two randomly chosen alleles from the pooled replicates started from the same genotype are identical in state. $C_{1}$ is related to Wright’s Fis statistic as:

$$
F_{is}≡F_{rg}≡\frac{Q_{r}-Q_{g}}{1-Q_{g}}
$$



$$
1-F_{rg}=\frac{1-Q_{g}-Q_{r}+Q_{g}}{1-Q_{g}}=\frac{1-Q_{r}}{1-Q_{g}}
$$



$$
\frac{1}{1-F_{rg}}=\frac{1-Q_{g}}{1-Q_{r}}=C_{1}
$$

We used count data from Illumina sequencing to estimate allele frequencies and followed the approach of Hivert et al., 2018, which developed a methods of moments estimator, $F^_{st}^{pool}$, that is appropriate for pooled data and accounts for both the sampling of individuals within a population and the sampling of reads during sequencing. We treated each amino acid site independently and defined the following:

$$
R_{1:rgs}≡# of reads in replicate r of starting genotype g at site s
$$



$$
\pi^_{a:rgs}≡ observed allele frequency of allele a in replicate r of starting genotype g at site s
$$



$$
\pi^_{a:gs}≡ observed allele frequency of allele a in pooled replicates of starting genotype g at site s
$$

Using these values, we used the estimator of $F^_{st}^{pool}$ defined in Hivert et al., 2018 to estimate $F_{rg}$ for a single site:

$$
F^_{st}^{pool}≡F^_{rg}^{s}≡\frac{MSG_{gs}-MSR_{gs}}{MSG_{gs}+ℛ_{gs}-1MSR_{gs}}
$$

where:

$MSG_{gs}≡\frac{1}{R_{1:gs}−R_{2:gs}}\suma=121\sumr=1n_{r:g}R_{1:rgs}(\pi^_{a:rgs}−\pi^_{a:gs})^{2}$ is the mean sum-of-squares for pooled replicates.

$MSR_{gs}≡\frac{1}{R_{1:gs}−R_{1:gs}}\suma=121\sumr=1n_{r:g}R_{1:rgs}\pi^_{a:rgs}(1−\pi^_{a:rgs})$ is the mean sum-of-squares within replicates.

$R_{gs}≡\frac{R_{1:gs}−\frac{R_{2:gs}}{R_{1:gs}}}{R_{1:gs}−R_{2:gs}}$, is the effective number of individuals after accounting for sampling, with

$$
R_{1:gs}≡\sumr=1n_{r:g}R_{1:rgs},R_{2:gs}≡\sumr=1n_{r:g}R_{1:rgs}^{2}R_{1:gs}≡\sumr=1n_{r:g}\frac{R_{1:rgs}+n_{i:rg}−1}{n_{i:rg}},
$$

and

$$
R_{2:gs}≡\frac{1}{R_{1:gs}}\sumr=1n_{r:g}\frac{R_{1:rgs}(R_{1:rgs}+n_{i:rg}−1)}{n_{i:rg}}.
$$

Here, $n_{r:g}$ is the number of replicates started from genotype $g$ and $n_{i:rg}$ is the number of individual phage in replicate $r$ of starting genotype $g$ in the sample used to make the sequencing library.

From the relationship between $C_{1}$ and $F_{rg}$, we approximated the site-specific effects of chance for a particular starting genotype as:

$$
C^_{1:g}^{s}≡\frac{1}{1−F^_{rg}^{s}}=\frac{1}{1−\frac{MSG_{gs}−MSR_{gs}}{MSG_{gs}+(R_{gs}−1)MSR_{gs}}}=\frac{1}{\frac{MSG_{gs}+(R_{gs}−1)MSR_{gs}−MSG_{gs}+MSR_{gs}}{MSG_{gs}+(R_{gs}−1)MSR_{gs}}}=\frac{MSG_{gs}+(R_{gs}−1)MSR_{gs}}{R_{gs}MSR_{gs}}=1+\frac{MSG_{gs}−MSR_{gs}}{R_{gs}MSR_{gs}}
$$

When there were replicates from more than one starting genotype, we calculated $MSG_{gs}$, $MSR_{gs}$, and $R_{gs}$ separately for each starting genotype and averaged these values together, using weights proportional to the number of replicates for that genotype. Thus:

$$
C^_{1}^{s}=1+\frac{\sumg=1n_{g}n_{r:g}\sumg=1n_{g}n_{r:g}(MSG_{gs}−MSR_{gs})}{\sumg=1n_{g}n_{r:g}R_{gs}\sumg=1n_{g}n_{r:g}MSR_{gs}}
$$

where $n_{g}$ is the number of distinct starting genotypes.

We then took the average numerator and average denominator as suggested by Hivert et al., 2018 and Weir and Cockerham, 1984 for estimating $F_{st}$:

$$
C^_{1}=1+\frac{\sums=1n_{s}\sumg=1n_{g}n_{r:g}\sumg=1n_{g}n_{r:gs}(MSG_{gs}−MSR_{gs})}{\sums=1n_{s}\sumg=1n_{g}n_{r:g}R_{gs}\sumg=1n_{g}n_{r:g}MSR_{gs}}
$$

where $n_{s}$ is the number of sites.

#### Estimating the effects of contingency

To determine the effects of contingency ($C_{2}$) on the outcomes of evolution, we compared the average allele frequency of replicate PACE experiments between different starting genotypes. For each starting genotype, we pooled all replicates started from that genotype and treated it as a single sample. We compared allele frequencies among genotypes by estimating the probability that two randomly chosen alleles in a sample would be different if they were both drawn from the same starting genotype $(V_{g})$ or drawn from different starting genotypes $(V_{t})$:

$$
C_{2}≡\frac{V_{t}}{V_{g}}≡\frac{1−Q_{g1\neqg2}}{1−Q_{g1=g2}}
$$

where $Q_{g1=g2}$ is the probability that two randomly chosen alleles from the same starting genotype are identical in state and $Q_{g1\neqg2}$ is the probability that two randomly chosen alleles from different starting genotypes are identical in state. To calculate $1−Q_{g1\neqg2}$, we note that the probability of two randomly drawn alleles being different when chosen irrespective of starting genotype is simply the average of the probability of two randomly drawn alleles being different when they are drawn from the same and different starting genotypes, that is:

$$
(1−Q_{t})=\frac{1}{2}(1−Q_{g1=g2})+\frac{1}{2}(1−Q_{g1\neqg2})
$$

where $Q_{t}$ is the probability that two randomly chosen alleles irrespective of starting genotype are identical in state. From this we have:

$$
2(1−Q_{t})=(1−Q_{g1=g2})+(1−Q_{g1\neqg2})
$$



$$
(1−Q_{g1\neqg2})=2(1−Q_{t})−(1−Q_{g1=g2})
$$



$$
(1−Q_{g1\neqg2})=1−2Q_{t}+Q_{g1=g2}
$$

Using this and the fact that $Q_{g1=g2}$ is equivalent to $Q_{g}$ used above to calculate the effects of chance, we have:

$$
C_{2}=\frac{1−2Q_{t}+Q_{g1=g2}}{1−Q_{g1=g2}}=\frac{1−Q_{t}}{1−Q_{g1=g2}}+\frac{Q_{g1=g2}−Q_{t}}{1−Q_{g1=g2}}=\frac{1−Q_{t}}{1−Q_{g}}+\frac{Q_{g}−Q_{t}}{1−Q_{g}}
$$

This statistic is related to Wright’s Fst as:

$$
F_{st}≡F_{gt}≡\frac{Q_{g}−Q_{t}}{1−Q_{t}}
$$



$$
1−F_{gt}=\frac{1−Q_{t}−Q_{g}+Q_{t}}{1−Q_{t}}=\frac{1−Q_{g}}{1−Q_{t}}
$$

and

$$
1+F_{gt}=\frac{1−Q_{t}}{1−Q_{t}}+\frac{Q_{g}−Q_{t}}{1−Q_{t}}
$$



$$
\frac{1+F_{gt}}{1−F_{gt}}=\frac{\frac{1−Q_{t}}{1−Q_{t}}+\frac{Q_{g}−Q_{t}}{1−Q_{t}}}{\frac{1−Q_{g}}{1−Q_{t}}}=\frac{1−Q_{t}}{1−Q_{g}}+\frac{Q_{g}−Q_{t}}{1−Q_{g}}
$$

As with the effects of chance, we used the method of moments estimator defined in Hivert et al., 2018 to estimate the effects of contingency:

$$
F^_{gt}≡\frac{MST_{s}−MSG_{s}}{MST_{s}+(R_{ts}−1)MSG_{s}}
$$

where:

$MST_{s}≡\frac{1}{R_{1:s}−R_{2:s}}\suma=121\sumg=1n_{g}R_{1:gs}(\pi^_{a:gs}−\pi^_{a:s})^{2}$ is the mean sum-of-squares for the entire pooled sample.

$MSG_{s}≡\frac{1}{R_{1:s}−R_{1:s}}\suma=121\sumg=1n_{g}R_{1:gs}\pi^_{a:gs}(1−\pi^_{a:gs})$ is the mean sum-of-squares for a starting genotype.

$R_{ts}≡\frac{R_{1:s}−\frac{R_{2:s}}{R_{1:s}}}{R_{1:s}−R_{2:s}}$, is the effective number of individuals after accounting for sampling, with

$\pi^_{a:s}≡ the observed allele frequency of allele  a among all genotypes at site s$,

$$
R_{1:s}≡\sumg=1n_{g}R_{1:gs},
$$



$$
R_{2:s}≡\sumg=1n_{g}R_{1:gs}^{2},
$$



$$
R_{1:s}≡\sumg=1n_{g}\frac{R_{1:gs}+n_{i:g}−1}{n_{i:g}},
$$

and

$$
R_{2:s}≡\frac{1}{R_{1:s}}\sumg=1n_{g}\frac{R_{1:gs}(R_{1:gs}+n_{i:g}−1)}{n_{i:g}}.
$$

With $n_{i:g}$ being the number of individual phage used to make the libraries for starting genotype $g$.

From the relationship between $F_{gt}$ and $C_{2}$, we approximated the effects of contingency as:

$$
C^_{2}^{s}=\frac{1+F^_{gt}^{s}}{1−F^_{gt}^{s}}=\frac{1+\frac{MSP_{ts}−MSI_{ts}}{MSP_{ts}+(R_{ts}−1)MSI_{ts}}}{1−\frac{MSP_{ts}−MSI_{ts}}{MSP_{ts}+(R_{ts}−1)MSI_{ts}}}
$$



$$
=\frac{\frac{MSP_{ts}+(R_{ts}−1)MSI_{ts}+MSP_{ts}−MSI_{ts}}{MSP_{ts}+(R_{ts}−1)MSI_{ts}}}{\frac{MSP_{ts}+(R_{ts}−1)MSI_{ts}−MSP_{ts}+MSI_{ts}}{MSP_{ts}+(R_{ts}−1)MSI_{ts}}}
$$



$$
=\frac{MSP_{ts}+(R_{ts}−1)MSI_{ts}+MSP_{ts}−MSI_{ts}}{MSP_{ts}+(R_{ts}−1)MSI_{t}s−MSP_{ts}+MSI_{ts}}
$$



$$
=\frac{R_{ts}MSI_{ts}+2MSP_{ts}−2MSI_{ts}}{R_{ts}MSI_{ts}}
$$



$$
=1+2\frac{MSP_{ts}−MSI_{ts}}{R_{ts}MSI_{ts}}
$$

Again, we treated all sites as independent and summed the numerator and denominators to estimate the effects of contingency:

$$
C^_{2}=1+2\frac{\sums=1n_{s}(MSP_{ts}−MSI_{ts})}{\sums=1n_{s}R_{ts}MSI_{ts}}
$$

#### Estimating the combined effect of chance and contingency

To determine the combined effects of chance and contingency $(C_{3})$ on the outcomes of evolution, we compared allele frequencies from individual replicates to the average allele frequency among replicates from different starting genotypes. In each case, we pooled replicates started from a genotype and treated it as a single sample and compared it to the individual replicates started from different genotypes. We compared allele frequencies by estimating the probability that two randomly chosen alleles would be different if they were both drawn from the same replicate or if they were drawn from a different starting genotype:

$$
C_{3}≡\frac{1−Q_{g1\neqg2}}{1−Q_{r}}=\frac{1−Q_{g}}{1−Q_{r}}∗\frac{1−Q_{g1\neqg2}}{1−Q_{g}}=C_{1}∗C_{2}=\frac{V_{t}}{V_{r}}
$$

We thus used:

$$
C^_{3}=C^_{1}∗C^_{2}
$$

as our estimate of the combined effects of chance and contingency. This estimator indicates that the combined effects of chance and contingency are multiplicative and thus amplify each other’s effects as they get larger.

Acceptance summary:

This manuscript presents an original, clever, high throughput, and rapid experimental protein evolution method to assess the roles and contributions of contingency, chance, and necessity in the evolution of protein-protein interactions. The authors focus on the animal BCL-2 protein family and on the evolution of their binding properties to two proteins, NOXA and BID. Using several replicates and several starting points, they found little predictability between replicates of single starting points and among those from multiple starting points, indicating that there is no single pathway through sequence space to the selected function, and that historical contingency is here the primary cause of protein evolution. Reviewer #3 (Recommendations for the authors):

To flesh out my comment about needing to engage the conceptual work that has been done on contingency, I have two major issues I would like to see dealt with:

First, contingency and chance are discussed by the authors as being separate, but they are not. Indeed, chance is a critical component of contingency. Some more engagement with the philosophers who have specialized in this area, especially John Beatty, Eric Desjardins and Alison McConwell. They have made clear that contingency is not just causal dependence. Beatty, for instance, has articulated how contingent outcomes are not simply those that stem from earlier events, but depend on pasts with chance components so that their occurrence was not guaranteed. (See Beatty, and Carrera, When what had to happen was not bound to happen: History, chance, narrative, evolution. Journal of the Philosophy of History 5: 471-495. 2011.) Unless chance is involved in the causal paths taken over time from a given start to a given beginning, then there is not really any contingency, but merely determinism. Desjardins has elaborated this further into understanding contingency in the context of path dependence (See Desjardins, Historicity and Experimental Evolution. Biol. Philos. 26, 339-364, 2011 And Desjardins, Reflections on path dependence and irreversibility: Lessons from evolutionary biology. Philosophy of Science 78: 724 – 738, 2017.) The passage in the introduction that, "…if diversity reflects contingency-a strong dependence of future events on past and current states-then the outcomes of evolution would be predictable only given complete knowledge of the constraints and opportunities specific to each starting point" is therefore incorrect, because contingency involves not just dependence on starting conditions. Contingency makes for broader unpredictability because indeterminacy, such as that introduced by the randomness of mutations, is characteristic of the causal chain no matter the starting point. (This point, incidentally, is made in the Blount et al., 2018 and Beatty, 2009 papers cited to support the quoted statement.) Similarly, the conclusion, then, that "Conversely, without chance, contingency in history would be inconsequential, because all phylogenetic lineages launched from a common ancestor would always lead to the same intermediate steps and thus the same ultimate outcomes" is well stated, but it misses that contingency without chance is not contingency. It misses, therefore, sophisticated conceptual elaboration of what exactly what contingency really involves. I think the arguments made about what the experimental findings mean would be better if that work were taken into account. The study of contingency is rife with conceptual mix-ups and crosstalk, and it is critical to engage what the philosophers have done to clarify things and help us scientists out so that we can really all be on the same page.

My second issue is related. The work deals with chance, contingency, and necessity in the evolution of protein sequence. However, there is little grappling with how contingency actually matters if it simply means that proteins can evolve along many different paths depending on historical substitutions to the same function. If there are multiple paths to functionally equivalent end states, how do they matter? Such convergence is in line with Conway Morris's argument that contingency does not matter because, "the routes are many, but the destinations are limited." Indeed, if there really are a fantastically large number of alternate paths that can be taken to the same end, then the role for contingency in the final state is actually minimal. Where it could matter would be if 1. There were end functional states reachable via different pathways that were qualitatively similar, but not actually the same, and/or 2. The end states vary in their potential for later evolution. As it stands, the manuscript leaves me unable to see how it matters if "Present-day proteins are physical anecdotes of the particular unpredictable histories", but all those anecdotes have the same punchlines and meanings. Now, I will state outright that I think that history does play a role beyond simply the contingency of evolutionary paths to the same destination, but there is a functionally convergent, non-contingent elephant in the room with which the authors need to engage.

results.result: Prior to this study, the relative roles of chance, contingency, and necessity in evolution had not been assessed in a single system on timescales relevant to historical evolution, representing a major gap in evolutionary biology.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C8, C12, C14, C15, C16, C17, and C18 collectively establish the state of the field prior to this work. These claims are supported by citations to prior literature and logical arguments about the limitations of previous approaches. The authors accurately characterize the gap in knowledge that their study addresses.

results.result: The authors developed an experimental approach combining ancestral protein reconstruction with a new PACE system to evolve BCL-2 family proteins under selection for historically relevant protein-protein interaction specificities, allowing quantification of chance and contingency.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C24, C33, C34, C35, C36, C37, and C38 describe the experimental strategy. The approach is well-documented with methodological details, citations to prior work, and clear descriptions of how the design allows measurement of chance and contingency. The PACE system is validated experimentally (C57).

results.result: Ancestral protein reconstruction and experimental characterization revealed that BID specificity evolved in the BCL-2 clade when the ancestral ability to bind NOXA was lost between AncB2 and AncB4, and this reconstruction was robust to uncertainty in ancestral sequences.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C50 describe phylogenetic reconstruction and experimental validation of ancestral protein functions. The results are supported by multiple lines of evidence including luciferase assays (C42-C46), robustness tests with alternative reconstructions (C47), and corroboration with extant proteins from key phylogenetic positions (C48-C50). The experimental data with figures provide strong support.

results.result: All PACE trajectories (four replicates each from six starting genotypes) successfully evolved the target PPI specificities over approximately 100 rounds of viral replication, as confirmed by multiple experimental assays.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C64 describe the outcomes of PACE experiments. The success of all trajectories is documented with experimental validation using activity-dependent plaque assays and binding assays (C63), with references to figures. The observation of phenotypic variation within populations (C64) is consistent with prior PACE work and explained by population genetic factors (C65).

results.result: Necessity was almost entirely absent in PACE experiments: of 100 mutant states at 75 sites, 73 appeared in only one trajectory, and only four arose in multiple replicates from multiple starting points. The only universally acquired mutation had no detectable effect on binding.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C79 present quantitative results from deep sequencing analysis. The data are specific and well-documented (C68-C73), with experimental validation of the functionally neutral universal mutation (C73). The quantitative comparisons between trajectories from same vs. different starting points (C74-C77) provide clear evidence for both chance and contingency. The conclusion about unpredictability (C78) follows logically from the data.

results.result: PACE mutations rarely recapitulated or reversed historical substitutions that occurred during the interval when NOXA binding was lost, with only two reversions occurring exclusively in AncB4 trajectories and only in a subset of replicates.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C87 compare PACE mutations to historical substitutions. The results are specific and quantitative (C80-C82), with logical interpretations about contingency restricting accessibility (C83) and chance affecting outcomes even from the closest starting point (C84). The distinction between functionally relevant and irrelevant historical substitutions (C85-C86) is appropriately made. The conclusion (C87) is well-supported by the data.

results.result: Quantitative analysis of genetic variance revealed that chance increased variance by 30% (Vg/Vr), contingency by 80% (Vt/Vg), and their combined multiplicative effect by 2.4-fold (Vt/Vr), with no significant difference between gain and loss of interactions.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C92 present quantitative estimates of chance and contingency effects using genetic variance analysis. The analytical approach is clearly described (C88), the results are specific and quantitative (C89-C91), and the statistical framework appears sound. The multiplicative relationship (C91) is mathematically appropriate. The lack of difference between gain and loss experiments (C92) is noted with reference to a figure.

results.result: The effect of contingency increased significantly with phylogenetic distance while chance remained constant, resulting in contingency being three times greater than chance on the timescale of metazoan evolution, with a combined 3.2-fold increase in variance.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C99 describe how chance and contingency change over phylogenetic time using linear regression analysis. The results are specific and quantitative (C93-C98), with appropriate statistical analysis. The conclusion that contingency magnified by chance steadily increases unpredictability (C99) is well-supported by the data. The analysis appropriately accounts for phylogenetic structure.

results.result: Contingency arose through epistasis: mutations that conferred target specificities in their native backgrounds failed to do so in 11 of 12 swaps to other starting proteins, demonstrating that historical substitutions made specificity-changing mutations context-dependent.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C107 describe the mechanistic basis of contingency through mutation swap experiments. The experimental design is clear (C101-C102), with systematic testing showing all candidate mutations work in native backgrounds (C103) but fail in most other backgrounds (C104-C106). The only successful swap was between the most similar genotypes (C106). The conclusion about epistatic interactions (C107) is well-supported by the experimental data.

results.result: Both permissive and restrictive epistatic substitutions occurred on almost every phylogenetic branch, affecting both BID and NOXA binding, indicating that paths through sequence space changed repeatedly even during intervals when PPI binding profiles did not evolve.
results.evaluation: Claims C108-C113 map epistatic interactions onto the phylogeny. The results are specific about the distribution of epistatic effects (C108-C109), with appropriate characterization of the exceptional branch (C109-C111). The experimental demonstration that mutations fail to restore ancestral specificity even across the shortest branch (C112) strengthens the conclusion about changing mutational paths (C113).

results.result: Chance arose because multiple mutational paths to the selected specificity were accessible from each starting genotype, with partial determinism arising from structural constraints limiting the number of accessible routes for peptide binding.
results.evaluation: Claims C114-C123 dissect the mechanistic basis of chance. The experimental analysis of mutation effects in hsMCL-1 (C115-C118) demonstrates epistasis among permissive mutations, with structural analysis showing common mechanistic basis (C118). Similar patterns in other genotypes (C119) and structural mapping (C120-C121) support generality. The conclusions about multiple paths (C122) and structural constraints (C123) are well-supported by the data.

results.result: Under neutral evolution (selection for BID only), NOXA-binding variants arose at 0.1-1% frequency, with nearly all containing mutation r165L, which also appeared under direct selection, indicating that partial determinism arises from a limited number of mutations capable of conferring NOXA binding while retaining BID binding.
results.evaluation: Claims C124-C133 analyze the genetic basis of partial determinism through neutral evolution experiments. The experimental design is clear (C124-C125), with quantitative results on frequency (C126-C127) and specific mutations (C128-C129). The experimental validation of r165L's effect (C130) and observation of similar patterns in other genotypes (C131-C132) support the conclusion about limited mutational options (C133).

results.result: While all trajectories acquired historically relevant PPI specificities, contingency affected accessibility of non-historical functions: hsMCL-1 readily evolved NOXA-specific binding, but PACE-evolved hsBCL-2 variants with the same profile went extinct under the same selection.
results.evaluation: Claims C134-C140 demonstrate that contingency can affect functional accessibility. The success of all trajectories for historical functions (C134-C135) contrasts with differential success for non-historical functions (C136-C137). The control experiment (C138) rules out general lack of evolvability. The conclusions about contingency's influence (C139-C140) are well-supported by the experimental data.

results.result: Contingency generated over long historical timescales steadily erased necessity and overwhelmed chance as the primary cause of acquired sequence variation, making BCL-2 sequence evolution almost entirely unpredictable, with patterns of variation being idiosyncratic products of particular historical events.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C7 and C149-C154 present the main conclusions of the study. These are well-supported by the extensive experimental data on sequence outcomes (C68-C77), quantitative analysis of chance and contingency (C89-C99), mechanistic studies of epistasis (C100-C113), and analysis of mutational paths (C114-C133). The conclusions appropriately synthesize the multiple lines of evidence.

results.result: Chance and contingency are distinct but interacting modes of causality with a multiplicative relationship: chance determines which mutations occur from accessible sets, and contingency determines how those chance events shape future mutational accessibility, making evolution unpredictable.
results.evaluation: Claims C155-C163 present a conceptual framework for understanding the relationship between chance and contingency. The mathematical relationship (C157) is appropriate and supported by the quantitative analysis (C88-C91). The logical arguments about their interaction (C158-C163) are sound and well-supported by the experimental data showing both factors operating in the system.

results.result: The experimental design approximates but does not perfectly replicate historical evolution due to differences in population genetics, cellular context, and selection regimes, with some factors potentially underestimating and others potentially overestimating the historical roles of chance and contingency.
results.evaluation: Claims C164-C178 provide a thorough and balanced discussion of experimental limitations. The authors appropriately identify similarities (C165-C166) and differences (C167-C174) between their experiments and history, with thoughtful consideration of how these might bias results in different directions. The acknowledgment of uncertainty (C177) and scope limitations (C178) is appropriate. This represents good scientific practice in discussing limitations.

results.result: The results are expected to be qualitatively general to many proteins because epistasis is common and multiple mutational paths often exist, though the extent may vary with protein family, timescale, and functional constraints, with greater determinism expected for functions with narrow sequence-structure-function constraints.
results.evaluation: Claims C179-C183 discuss generalizability of the results. While the reasoning is sound and supported by citations to prior work (C180, C182, C183), these are speculative predictions about other systems rather than demonstrated results. The study examined one protein family, so claims about generality cannot be fully evaluated without additional data from other systems.

results.result: The developed PACE platform has several advantages for evolving PPI specificity: high-throughput parallel evolution across many generations in days, fewer components than previous methods making it easier to optimize, and simultaneous selection and counterselection for direct specificity evolution.
results.evaluation: Claims C184-C188 describe advantages of the methodological platform. The advantages are demonstrated by the successful experiments (C58-C64) and are supported by citations to prior work (C185). The comparison to alternative approaches (C186-C187) is reasonable. The prediction about broader applicability (C188) is appropriately framed as speculative.

results.result: Ancestral proteins were not more evolvable than extant proteins, with chance's effect constant across ~1 billion years, but the strong effect of contingency suggests that using multiple phylogenetically distant starting points would be most effective for protein engineering efforts.
results.evaluation: Claims C189-C192 discuss implications for protein engineering. The observation about ancestral evolvability (C189) is supported by the experimental data showing success from both ancestral and extant proteins. The constancy of chance (C190) is supported by the quantitative analysis (C94). The practical recommendations (C191-C192) follow logically from the demonstrated effects of contingency, though they remain to be tested in engineering applications.

results.result: Sequence-structure-function associations in alignments significantly reflect contingent constraints from chance historical events, requiring evolutionary explanations to explicitly consider historical trajectories rather than history-free approaches, with present-day proteins being physical anecdotes of their unpredictable histories.
results.evaluation: Claims C193-C197 present broader implications for evolutionary biology. These conclusions are well-supported by the experimental demonstration that sequence outcomes are highly contingent (C67-C79) and that epistatic interactions accumulate over time (C108-C113). The critique of history-free approaches (C194) is justified by the data. The characterization of proteins as 'physical anecdotes' (C195-C197) is a reasonable interpretation of the results, though somewhat philosophical.

results.result: The dominant paradigms of evolutionary biology (adaptationism and neutralism) focus on necessity or chance respectively, neither admitting much influence from contingency, and their dominance has obscured the possibility that contingency might be a primary factor shaping evolutionary outcomes.
results.evaluation: Claims C141-C148 characterize the historical context and dominant paradigms in evolutionary biology. These claims are supported by appropriate citations to foundational works and reviews. The characterization of the paradigms (C141-C145) is accurate, and the statement about recent work on contingency (C146-C147) is well-cited. The claim about paradigms obscuring contingency's role (C148) is a reasonable interpretation supported by citations.

results.result: The authors developed a novel PACE (phage-assisted continuous evolution) system using orthogonal split RNAPs to simultaneously select for and against specific protein-protein interactions. This system was applied to ancestral BCL-2 family proteins to evolve PPI specificities, with four replicates per starting genotype run for 4 days (~100 rounds of replication). The method allows rapid, high-throughput evolution with minimal intervention and can be extended to other protein families.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly praised the experimental setup as 'original, clever, high throughput, and rapid' and noted it 'shows a lot of potential for future studies of directed protein evolution in general.' The acceptance summary states the platform 'allows to simultaneously impose selection and counter-selection within the same cell,' confirming reviewers accepted the methodological innovation.

results.result: Ancestral protein reconstruction was used to infer the phylogeny of BCL-2 family proteins and reconstruct 12 ancestral proteins along lineages from AncMB1 (the common ancestor of BCL-2 and MCL-1 classes) to human BCL-2 and MCL-1. Experimental binding assays showed that AncMB1 and all MCL-1 clade ancestors bound both BID and NOXA, while BID specificity (loss of NOXA binding) evolved in the BCL-2 clade between AncB2 and AncB4 (ancestral deuterostome). This reconstruction was robust to uncertainty in ancestral sequences.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge the ancestral reconstruction methodology or the inferred evolutionary history of binding specificities. The acceptance summary acknowledges the study 'focus on the animal BCL-2 protein family and on the evolution of their binding properties to two proteins, NOXA and BID,' implicitly accepting the reconstructed evolutionary trajectory.

results.result: All PACE trajectories successfully acquired the target PPI specificities that were selected for, whether starting from promiscuous proteins (binding both BID and NOXA) or specific proteins (binding only BID). This was confirmed through activity-dependent plaque assays and in vivo/in vitro binding assays of randomly isolated phage clones.
results.evaluation: Reviewers stated 'The experiments are very nice, very well done, clearly presented and well interpreted' and noted that trajectories 'acquired the historically relevant PPI specificities.' No concerns were raised about the success of the PACE experiments in achieving the selected functions.

results.result: Deep sequencing revealed that necessity was almost entirely absent in PACE experiments. Of 100 mutant states at 75 sites that evolved to >5% frequency, 73 appeared in only a single trajectory, and only 4 arose in multiple replicates from multiple starting points. The only universally acquired mutation (nonsense at codon 271) had no detectable effect on binding. Trajectories from the same starting point differed at 78% of acquired states (chance), while those from different starting points differed at 92% (chance + contingency). Trajectories from phylogenetically distant proteins yielded virtually no common mutations despite identical selection pressures.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly accepted these findings, stating the authors 'found little predictability between replicates of single starting points and among those from multiple starting points, indicating that there is no single pathway through sequence space to the selected function.' The acceptance summary confirms 'historical contingency is here the primary cause of protein evolution.'

results.result: Genetic variance analysis quantified the relative effects of chance and contingency. Chance increased variance by 30% (Vg vs Vr), contingency by 80% (Vt vs Vg), and together by 2.4-fold (Vt vs Vr). Contingency's effect increased significantly with phylogenetic divergence, while chance's effect remained constant. On the timescale of metazoan evolution (~1 billion years), contingency's effect was three times greater than chance, with a combined 3.2-fold increase in variance.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge the quantitative variance analysis or the finding that contingency increases with phylogenetic distance. The acceptance summary acknowledges the study assessed 'the roles and contributions of contingency, chance, and necessity' without raising concerns about the quantitative framework.

results.result: Epistasis experiments revealed that contingency arose because historical substitutions made specificity-changing mutations either deleterious or inconsequential in different genetic backgrounds. All candidate causal mutation sets conferred the selected specificity in their native backgrounds, but 11 of 12 swaps into other backgrounds failed. Both permissive and restrictive epistatic substitutions occurred on almost every phylogenetic branch, affecting both BID and NOXA binding. The paths through sequence space leading to historical PPI specificities changed repeatedly during BCL-2 family history, even during intervals when binding profiles did not evolve.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not question the epistasis experiments or their interpretation. The acceptance summary's statement that 'historical contingency is here the primary cause of protein evolution' implicitly accepts the mechanistic explanation through epistasis.

results.result: Mechanistic analysis showed that chance arose because multiple mutational paths to the selected specificity were accessible from each starting genotype, while partial determinism arose because the number of accessible routes was limited by structure-function relationships. For example, mutation v189G required permissive mutations to decrease NOXA binding in hsMCL-1, and multiple sets of mutations could provide this effect. All repeatedly mutated sites either directly contacted the bound peptide or were on secondary structural elements that did so.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge the mechanistic explanations for chance and partial determinism. The detailed structural and functional analysis supporting these claims was not questioned in the reviews.

results.result: Neutral evolution experiments (selecting for BID binding without selection for/against NOXA) showed that variants fortuitously gaining NOXA binding arose at ~0.1-1% frequency. Nearly all sequenced clones contained mutation r165L, which also occurred at high frequency under direct selection for NOXA binding. Similar patterns were observed in AncB4 and AncB5, indicating that partial determinism arises because only a few mutations can confer NOXA binding while retaining BID binding.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not question the neutral evolution experiments or their interpretation regarding the limited number of mutations that can confer specific binding properties.

results.result: Experiments selecting for a non-historical function (binding NOXA but not BID) showed that hsMCL-1 readily evolved this phenotype, but two PACE-evolved hsBCL-2 variants with the same PPI profile went extinct under identical selection. This was not due to general lack of evolvability, as these variants successfully evolved to lose NOXA binding in separate experiments. This demonstrates that contingency can influence the accessibility of new functions and that the sequence encoding a functional phenotype affects subsequent phenotypic evolution.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge these experiments. Reviewer 3 raised a conceptual question about whether contingency matters if proteins evolve to 'functionally equivalent end states,' but this was a request for deeper engagement with the implications rather than a challenge to the experimental findings.

results.result: Comparison of PACE mutations to historical substitutions showed minimal recapitulation of historical changes. In experiments to lose NOXA binding, none of the acquired states recapitulated historical substitutions from the branch where NOXA binding was lost. In experiments to reacquire NOXA binding, only two states reversed historical substitutions, both occurring only in AncB4 (the immediate daughter node) and only in a subset of replicates. Some substitutions from other historical intervals were recapitulated, but these occurred when PPI specificity remained unchanged and thus could not have contributed to historical specificity changes.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge the comparison between PACE mutations and historical substitutions or the conclusion that chance and contingency strongly affected historical BCL-2 evolution.

results.result: Ancestral proteins showed no difference in evolvability compared to extant proteins—selected phenotypes readily evolved from both. Chance's effect was virtually constant across ~1 billion years of evolution, indicating that the number of accessible mutations conferring a selected function was apparently no greater in the deep past than now.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not question the finding that ancestral proteins are not more evolvable than extant proteins or that chance's effect remains constant over evolutionary time.

results.result: The authors acknowledge multiple limitations of their experimental design compared to historical evolution: population genetic parameters favor determinism (large populations, strong selection, high mutation rates); human BID and NOXA were used as fixed partners rather than co-evolving; PACE occurs in E. coli cytosol rather than animal cells with membrane-bound proteins; only two binding partners were tested rather than the full cellular context; peptide fragments were used rather than full-length proteins; and selection was for new specificities rather than purifying selection. Some differences may underestimate chance/contingency (e.g., stronger selection than in history), while others may overestimate them (e.g., additional cellular constraints in vivo).
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly requested that authors 'acknowledge the limitations of their study: BID and NOXA ancestral proteins were not used, peptides instead of full-length protein were used during interaction assays, proteins partially membrane-bound in vivo.' The main essential revision was to 'tone down their conclusions and broad claims' because 'the setup only allowed the authors to study the evolution of one protein family, considering only protein-protein interactions with few players, and in an artificial, bacterial environment.' This indicates reviewers found the limitations significant enough to warrant more cautious interpretation.

results.result: The authors conclude that patterns of variation in BCL-2 sequences (and likely other proteins) are idiosyncratic products of particular and unpredictable historical events. Present-day BCL-2 proteins are largely physical anecdotes of their unpredictable histories, reflecting the interaction of accumulated chance events with necessity imposed by physics, chemistry, and natural selection. Apparent 'design principles' reflect not how things must be to perform functions, but rather the legacy of opportunities and limitations inherited from history. Evolutionary explanations must explicitly consider historical trajectories rather than history-free approaches.
results.evaluation: Reviewers requested the authors 'tone down their conclusions and broad claims' and noted the study examined 'only one protein family, considering only protein-protein interactions with few players, and in an artificial, bacterial environment.' Reviewer 3 raised a conceptual concern about whether contingency matters if 'all those anecdotes have the same punchlines and meanings' (i.e., functional convergence), stating 'there is a functionally convergent, non-contingent elephant in the room with which the authors need to engage.' This indicates uncertainty about the broader implications and generalizability of the conclusions.

results.result: The authors present a conceptual framework distinguishing chance and contingency as distinct but interacting modes of causality. The total effect of both factors is multiplicative by definition. At any point in history, numerous mutation sets were accessible (chance determines which occurred), and these chance events then determined future accessible steps (contingency). Without chance, contingency would never be realized (all lineages would take the same path); without contingency, chance events would not affect accessibility of other mutations. Evolution is unpredictable when intermediate steps shape future possibilities (contingency) and those steps cannot be predicted (chance).
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 explicitly challenged the conceptual framework, stating 'contingency and chance are discussed by the authors as being separate, but they are not. Indeed, chance is a critical component of contingency.' The reviewer requested engagement with philosophical work (Beatty, Desjardins, McConwell) showing that 'contingency without chance is not contingency' and that the authors' treatment 'misses sophisticated conceptual elaboration of what exactly what contingency really involves.' This indicates the conceptual framework requires revision.

results.result: The authors speculate that qualitatively similar results may apply to many other proteins because epistasis is a common feature of protein structure and function, and the influence of chance depends on multiple mutational sets conferring new functions (likely common). However, they expect greater determinism for functions with narrow sequence-structure-function constraints (e.g., catalysis) than those with less strict requirements (e.g., substrate binding). Consistent with this, experimental evolution with diffuse selection on whole organisms has shown virtually no repeatability.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly stated the authors should 'tone down their conclusions and broad claims' because the study examined only 'one protein family' in 'an artificial, bacterial environment.' The request to acknowledge limitations and 'indicate further directions for follow-up studies' suggests reviewers found the generalization to other proteins premature without additional evidence.

results.result: The authors suggest practical implications for protein engineering: efforts to produce proteins with new functions by design or directed evolution will be most effective using multiple different protein sequences as starting points, ideally separated by long intervals of sequence evolution. Ancestral proteins can be useful simply because they provide routes to functions inaccessible from extant proteins, even if those routes are not fundamentally different in number or kind.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge these practical implications for protein engineering. The acceptance summary notes the method 'shows a lot of potential for future studies of directed protein evolution in general,' implicitly supporting the practical applications suggested.

comparisons.comparison: Perfect alignment on ancestral reconstruction claims (C39-C50). Both OpenEval and peer reviewers found the phylogenetic reconstruction and experimental validation of ancestral protein functions well-supported. No concerns raised about methodology or conclusions.

Perfect alignment on comparison of PACE mutations to historical substitutions (C80-C87). Both evaluations accepted the quantitative results and conclusions about contingency restricting accessibility and chance affecting outcomes.
Perfect alignment on neutral evolution experiments (C124-C133). Both evaluations supported the findings about partial determinism and limited mutational options for specific binding properties.

Strong disagreement on conceptual framework (C155-C163). OpenEval found the mathematical relationship and framework sound, but peer Reviewer 3 explicitly challenged the separation of chance and contingency, stating they are not separate and requesting engagement with philosophical literature.

Significant disagreement on limitations discussion (C164-C178). OpenEval praised the thorough acknowledgment of limitations as good scientific practice, but peer reviewers found limitations significant enough to require toning down conclusions and broad claims.

Agreement on uncertainty about generalizability (C179-C183). Both evaluations found claims about generality to other systems speculative. OpenEval noted lack of data from other systems; peer reviewers requested toning down broad claims due to single protein family study.

Strong alignment on mechanistic basis of chance (C114-C123, with C5-C6 in peer result). Both evaluations accepted the epistasis experiments, structural analysis, and conclusions about multiple paths and structural constraints.

Alignment on experimental findings for contingency affecting functional accessibility (C136-C140). Both accepted the experimental data, though peer reviewers raised conceptual questions about implications if proteins reach functionally equivalent end states.

Disagreement on broader implications (C193-C197, C7, C149). OpenEval found conclusions well-supported though somewhat philosophical, but peer reviewers requested toning down claims and raised concerns about functional convergence ('elephant in the room') that authors need to address.

Strong alignment on sequence unpredictability findings (C67-C79, with additional claims C3-C4, C150-C154 in peer result). Both evaluations accepted the quantitative deep sequencing results and conclusions about chance and contingency making outcomes unpredictable.

Alignment on quantitative variance analysis (C88-C99). Both evaluations accepted the analytical approach, quantitative estimates, and conclusions about how chance and contingency change over phylogenetic time.

Alignment on epistatic interactions underlying contingency (C100-C113). Both evaluations accepted the mutation swap experiments and conclusions about epistatic interactions accumulating over evolutionary time.

Alignment on ancestral evolvability findings (C189-C190). Both evaluations accepted that ancestral proteins are not more evolvable than extant proteins and that chance's effect remains constant over time.

Alignment on protein engineering implications (C191-C192). Both evaluations supported the practical recommendations, with peer reviewers noting the method shows potential for future directed evolution studies.
Alignment on mapping epistatic interactions onto phylogeny (C108-C113). Both evaluations accepted the experimental results and conclusions about changing mutational paths across evolutionary time.
Alignment on quantitative estimates of chance and contingency (C88-C92). Both evaluations accepted the genetic variance analysis framework and quantitative results without challenge.

Strong alignment on experimental strategy and PACE platform (C2, C24, C33-C38, with additional methodological claims in peer result). Both evaluations praised the experimental design as original, clever, and well-validated, with peer reviewers noting high potential for future studies.

Partial alignment on main conclusions (C3-C7, C149-C154). Both accepted the experimental support for conclusions about unpredictability, but peer result focuses on sequence-level findings while OpenEval also addresses broader synthesis.

Alignment on methodological advantages (C184-C188). Both evaluations accepted the advantages of the platform, with peer reviewers explicitly praising it as original and high-throughput with potential for future studies.

Alignment on PACE experimental outcomes (C58-C64, with C62-C63 and C134-C135 in peer result). Both evaluations accepted that trajectories successfully acquired selected functions and that experiments were well-executed.
